Chapter 1: Growing Up in a World of Politics and Family Expectations.
Sometimes, the road to power really does start in the most ordinary places—right at the kitchen table, in a bustling family home, or maybe on a neighborhood block where everyone seems to know your name.
Imagine a young girl in the heart of Baltimore, watching her father—a local politician—move through the everyday rhythms of public life. Their house was never quiet. Neighbors would drop in hoping for help, party workers came to strategize, and siblings were always competing for a little attention.
For her, politics wasn’t just some far-off concept. It was as much a part of daily life as the scent of Sunday dinner drifting from the kitchen.
She figured out early that true public service goes way beyond speeches or shaking hands. It’s about really listening to people’s worries, looking for answers, and never ignoring a knock at the door.
Her mother, too, was a quiet force—keeping the household running, standing behind her husband’s ambitions, and showing her daughter just how important resilience can be.
In that busy home, the lessons came fast. Loyalty. Hard work. And maybe most of all, the importance of showing up—even when you’d rather not.
As she grew up, the expectations around her didn’t need to be spelled out. There was pride in the family name, sure, but also this sense of duty that lingered in the air.
Watching her father handle the wild world of city politics, she saw that success took more than just charm. You needed a certain toughness, too.
And Baltimore itself? It was like a living classroom—full of contradictions. Wealth and poverty, hope and disappointment, progress right alongside prejudice.
Those early days helped her understand that power isn’t just handed out. It’s earned, and protected, and—maybe most importantly—used to lift up others.
School brought its own set of challenges. In classrooms where boys dominated the conversation, she learned to speak up, even when her voice shook a little.
Some teachers assumed she’d take the traditional route, but she had other plans. She wanted a future that honored her family’s story, but also blazed a new path.
Friendships came and went, but those lessons about loyalty and sticking with it? They stayed.
Back at home, the family’s Catholic faith was a steady guide. The rituals and teachings brought comfort, but also sparked big questions—about justice, compassion, and what it meant to be a woman in the world.
She saw her mother’s quiet strength and couldn’t help but wonder why there weren’t more women in charge.
Ambition took root, even if she didn’t quite know what to do with it yet.
By the time she packed up for college, she carried a deep sense of responsibility. The world outside was changing—civil rights marches filled the streets, politics were shifting, and new doors were opening for women.
At first, she just watched from the sidelines, not sure where she fit into the bigger story.
But those early lessons—about persistence, adaptability, and believing that one person really can make a difference—were always there to guide her.
These first years laid down the foundation for a life spent at the crossroads of personal conviction and public service.
The journey ahead would be long, sometimes even tough, but the values shaped by her family and community? They’d turn out to be her strongest assets.
